terminal_record.title: Vought Ordered CFPB Staff to Stop Work; Court Blocked Further Layoffs
terminal_record.description_short: Vought ordered CFPB staff to stop work on Feb. 10, 2025; a judge blocked more layoffs after over 100 workers had been fired.
terminal_record.description_medium: On February 10, 2025, Acting CFPB Director Russell Vought ordered bureau employees to stop work. A federal judge later blocked additional layoffs after more than 100 workers had been fired that week. The sources support a work stoppage and workforce reduction effort, but do not substantiate the frozen entry’s claim that all roughly 1,700 employees were fired on February 7.
terminal_record.description_long: On February 10, 2025, CFPB Acting Director Russell Vought ordered bureau employees to stop work, according to the District Court’s later account in NTEU v. Vought. The court said the administration was pursuing measures to dismantle the agency, including firings, funding cuts, contract terminations, office closures and a reduction in force. On February 14, NPR reported that a federal judge blocked additional layoffs after more than 100 workers had already been fired that week. The record therefore describes a serious work stoppage and attempted workforce reduction, not a completed firing of the bureau’s full roughly 1,700-person staff. The original February 7 date is not the date of the stop-work order identified in the opinion, and the sources reviewed do not establish that all pending CFPB cases were halted. The injunction was preliminary while litigation continued; it does not by itself decide every underlying legal question. This correction preserves the CFPB action and its immediate legal response while separating completed events from planned reductions. The supplied claim that the bureau’s closure benefited Trump campaign donors is not supported by the sources cited here and is omitted.
organization_tags: U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia

terminal_record.title: Supplied allegation: FISA surveillance monitored journalists’ government sources in March 2025
terminal_record.description_short: The supplied record alleges March 2025 FISA surveillance of journalists’ communications with government sources.
terminal_record.description_medium: An unverified supplied account alleges that in March 2025 the Trump administration used FISA warrants to monitor communications between national-security reporters and government sources, potentially exposing confidential contacts and reporters to prosecution. The packet names no journalist, warrant, agency, or docket, and supplies no source establishing the surveillance or attribution. The date remains provisional, and publication is ineligible.
terminal_record.description_long: The supplied account alleges that in March 2025 the Trump administration used warrants under FISA to monitor communications between reporters covering national-security matters and government officials who served as sources. It frames the alleged monitoring as an effort to identify confidential reporting contacts and says the information could expose journalists to prosecution for their newsgathering. These are allegations supplied in the packet; this draft does not establish that a warrant existed, that the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court authorized one against a journalist, that surveillance occurred, or that any reporter or source was identified. The packet names Donald Trump, Kash Patel, and Pam Bondi but provides no specific role or order linking any of them to a warrant, so this draft does not assign individual responsibility. It identifies no journalist, government source, agency, case, application, or court docket. March 1 is retained only as provisional packet timing. Until those details have claim-level evidence, the entry should remain internal drafting material and cannot support publication or a conclusion that press freedom was harmed.
